transcript.content: Hi, it’s good to meet you. What brings you in today?

Hi, nice to meet you too. Um, well, I came in because I just feel... I feel so incredibly worn out, all the time. It's not just like regular tiredness, you know? It's like this deep, heavy exhaustion that never goes away. Like, I'll go to bed, try to get a full eight hours, sometimes even more if I can manage it, but when I wake up, it doesn't even matter. It feels like my body is literally made of sandbags. Just getting out of bed is a monumental task. And then, trying to get through my workday—I'm a market research analyst, so I really have to be sharp and focused, looking at data and trends—but lately, it just takes everything I have just to stare at the screen. Even the little things at home, like... I was trying to fold laundry the other day, just a small basket of towels and shirts, and I felt like I had run a marathon by the time I was halfway through. I had to sit down on the edge of the bed and just stare at the wall. It’s just so draining, this constant lack of energy, and it’s really starting to affect how I function on a day-to-day basis. I just don't know why I can't seem to shake it, no matter how much rest I get.
After you do even a small amount of physical or mental activity, do you feel significantly worse afterward?

Um, I don't think so? I mean, I wouldn't say I feel *worse* afterward, exactly. It's not really a crash that happens after the fact. It's more like... the exhaustion is just always there, sitting on me at the exact same heavy level, whether I'm doing something or not. 

Like, if I finally manage to finish looking through a huge dataset at work—which, by the way, takes me like three times as long right now because I just can't keep my eyes focused on the rows and columns, it's all just a blur of consumer demographics and percentages—but when I finally get to the end of a report and close the laptop, I don't suddenly feel a new wave of fatigue. I'm just exactly as completely drained as I was when I started. It's almost like driving a car with a completely empty gas tank, you know? You're not losing more gas by pressing the pedal because there just wasn't any to begin with. I just stay at this constant, miserable zero all day long. 

So, no, finishing the laundry or getting through a long Zoom meeting doesn't make the physical heaviness worse afterward, it's just... my baseline is already so incredibly low right now. I keep trying to explain it to my sister, and she keeps asking if I "overdid it" on the weekends, and I have to keep telling her, I didn't actually *do* anything to overdo it! I just always feel this way before, during, and after whatever it is I'm trying to accomplish. So yeah, I wouldn't say it gets worse after an activity, it's just a flatline of being totally worn out.
Have you been feeling down or depressed lately?

Yeah, I have... I really have. It's, um, it's hard to separate it from the exhaustion sometimes, but it's definitely there, and it's really overwhelming. Most days, honestly, I wake up and before I even try to move my arms or legs, I just have this... this incredibly heavy, flat feeling sitting right in the middle of my chest. It's almost like a physical weight, but it's an emotional one, if that makes sense? 

I'll finally drag myself out of bed and shuffle into the kitchen to make coffee, though half the time I don't even end up drinking it because I just don't care enough to take a sip. But I'll sit there at my kitchen table—it's this little round oak table I bought a few years ago at an antique fair, I usually love sitting there in the mornings—and I'll just stare out the back window at the yard. The grass is getting way too long right now because I haven't had it in me to deal with it, but I just sit there staring at the weeds for what feels like hours. 

And while I'm sitting there, my brain just goes to these incredibly empty places. I just sit there and feel like... like there is absolutely no good version of the future coming. I try to think about next week, or next month, or even just the upcoming weekend, and it's all just this bleak, gray wall. I can't picture anything getting better, or anything good happening with my research projects at work, or even just having a normal, pleasant afternoon. It's just this overwhelming sense that everything is pointless. So yeah, I guess feeling down is an understatement, because it's not just being sad, it's this complete lack of hope that just sits in my chest every single morning while I'm looking out at that overgrown lawn.
Before this current period, have you ever had another time in your life when you felt depressed like this for at least two weeks?

Um, no... no, I don't think so. I mean, I've had times where I felt sad, you know? Like when my dog passed away a few years ago—he was this sweet little beagle mix named Buster, I had him for almost twelve years—I was devastated then. I cried for days and I didn't want to do anything, but that felt different because there was a very clear reason for it. I was grieving. And eventually, after a few weeks, the sharpness of it faded and I started to feel like myself again, even though I still missed him. 

But this... this heavy, completely empty feeling where I can't even picture a future? No, I've never had a period like this before. I've always been pretty driven, honestly. Like I said, my job requires a lot of focus, and I've always been the kind of person who could just push through stress or a bad week. Even when I was going through my divorce in my late twenties, which was incredibly stressful and upsetting, I never felt this absolute deadness inside. I was angry, I was hurt, but I wasn't... hollowed out like this. So, no, I really can't recall any other time in my life where I felt this deeply depressed for weeks on end for no real reason. This is entirely new, and that's part of why it's so terrifying, to be honest. It just feels like it came out of nowhere and set up camp.
Have you had thoughts of killing yourself?

Um... I... I don't know if I'd say I want to kill myself, exactly, but... but things have gotten really dark in my head lately. Especially at night. The nights are the worst, honestly. My husband, Mark—he works these really long shifts sometimes, he's a physical therapist and he takes on extra hours at this rehabilitation clinic across town, so he doesn't get home until after nine on Tuesdays and Thursdays. And on those nights, when it's just me in the house, the quiet just gets so loud, if that makes sense? 

I'll be sitting on the couch, wrapped in this old fleece blanket we've had since we first got married, and the TV will be on, maybe some home improvement show or something mindless, but I'm not really watching it. And my mind just starts wandering down these really awful paths. I start thinking about how much of a burden I am right now. I mean, he's working so hard, and I'm just sitting here, barely able to function, barely able to pull together a basic grocery list, let alone contribute to our life the way I used to. 

And then... then I catch myself thinking that maybe he'd just be better off without me. Like, if I just wasn't here anymore, he wouldn't have to deal with this heavy, miserable version of me. He could just move on and have a normal life with someone who actually has the energy to go out to dinner or, you know, hold a conversation that isn't just about how tired they are. 

I haven't... I haven't made a plan or anything like that. I'm not sitting there figuring out how to do it. But it's just this recurring thought that creeps in. Like, "he would be so much lighter if I were gone." And it keeps coming back. It happens often enough now that it really scares me, because I never used to think like that. I used to be the one planning our vacations and dragging him out to try new restaurants, and now I'm just sitting in the dark thinking he'd be better off if I just disappeared. So, yeah, I guess... I guess those thoughts are there, and they're really frightening to me.
Have you lost interest or pleasure in things you usually enjoy?

Yeah, I have. I really, really have, and it's... it's honestly one of the most frustrating parts of all this. Because I used to be someone who was always doing something, you know? Like, my weekends were always booked. I used to love hiking. Mark and I would go up to the state park—there's this one trail, the Pine Ridge trail, it's about a four-mile loop with this gorgeous overlook at the halfway point—and we used to do that at least twice a month. I haven't been in... I can't even tell you how long. I just keep canceling. He'll ask if I want to go on a Saturday morning, and I just look at my boots by the door and the thought of putting them on just feels like climbing a mountain itself. 

And it's not just the hiking. I used to do yoga three mornings a week. I had this great little routine in the living room before work, but my mat has been rolled up in the corner for weeks. I look at it and I just feel... nothing. No desire to unroll it. Same with my garden. I mentioned the lawn earlier, but my actual flower beds are a disaster right now. I usually take so much pride in my perennials, I have these beautiful daylilies and some coneflowers that I planted from seed, but they're getting choked out by weeds because I just don't care enough to go out there with my trowel. 

And probably the saddest thing for me is my photography. I love taking bird photos. I have this really nice Nikon camera, I saved up for a year to buy this specific telephoto lens so I could get good shots of the goldfinches and cardinals that come to our feeders. I used to sit out on the back patio for hours on Sunday afternoons just waiting for the perfect shot. But lately... my camera is just sitting in its case in the hall closet. I know it's there, I know the birds are out there, but I just can't bring myself to take it out. None of it—the hiking, the yoga, the garden, the photography—none of it feels worth the effort anymore. It just feels like going through the motions, and I don't have the energy to fake it. So I just don't do any of it.
Have you been hearing or seeing things that other people don’t, or strongly believing something that others say isn’t true?

No, no, nothing like that. I mean, my mind can get pretty dark, like I was saying about those nights when Mark is working late and I'm just sitting there on the couch, but I'm definitely not hallucinating or anything. I know what's real and what isn't. I don't hear voices or see things that aren't there. 

Like, I know some people with really severe depression or other issues can have that happen, where they lose touch with reality, but that's not me. I'm very grounded in reality, almost too much, you know? Like, I'm painfully aware of everything around me, the messy house, the weeds in the garden, the silence. It's just that my perspective on it all is so incredibly bleak right now. 

And as for believing things that aren't true... well, I guess the only thing is that feeling I mentioned, the one where I think Mark would be better off without me. Sometimes that feels like an absolute fact in my head. Like, I'll be sitting there and it just feels so true, like I'm this anchor dragging him down. But... even then, if I really force myself to step back and look at it logically, which is hard to do right now, I know he loves me. I know he'd be devastated if something happened to me. He tells me all the time that we're a team and we'll get through this. So, even though my brain tries to convince me I'm worthless and he'd be happier if I were gone, I know, deep down, that it's just the depression talking. It's not a delusion, it's just... it's just this incredibly heavy guilt and sadness. But no, no actual hallucinations or bizarre beliefs like that. Just... just my own horrible thoughts.
